measurement.mode: static Vite client bundle graph — no browser, no network, no rendering
measurement.browser: not applicable. The gate never launches a browser; it reads the chunk graph the Vite build emits (dist/client/bundle-graph.json) and sums, per route, the client entry chunk, the static-import closure of the route's own chunk, and the chunks of its layout ancestors (a nested route renders its parent layouts). Browser-dependent behaviour is out of scope by design — see Issue #384 (Lighthouse measurement) and #385 (score gate).
measurement.network: not applicable. Budgeted numbers are RAW on-disk bytes of the files a browser must fetch before the route is interactive. gzip -9 figures are printed for reference only and are never budgeted, because a CDN's compression settings are not part of this measurement.
measurement.cpu: not time-based. The measurement is byte arithmetic over a build artefact, so it is deterministic on any machine and independent of runner speed. Only the wall-clock cost of `pnpm run build` that produces the artefact is runner-dependent.
measurement.source_sha: the commit the run is executed at, printed as `git rev-parse HEAD`. In CI the client build and this check run in the same job against the same SHA, so a red run always names the exact tree that was measured; locally, rebuild before rerunning if the tree changed. The gate also warns (it does not fail) when the graph's recorded client assets no longer exist under its own out_dir, which is what a stale or foreign `dist/client/bundle-graph.json` looks like.
measurement.reproduce_locally: pnpm run build && pnpm run bundle:budget:check
measurement.reproduce_in_ci: the `validate` job of .github/workflows/ci.yml runs `pnpm run validate:integration`, which runs this check immediately after `pnpm run build:production`.

headroom_policy:
Every JS cap in this file is the formula output of ONE measurement: the measured `initial_js_bytes` plus at least 0.35% headroom, rounded up to the next multiple of 5,000 bytes — `ceil(measured * 1.0035 / 5000) * 5000`. There is one shared CSS cap for the same reason there is one entry chunk: the initial stylesheet is a single asset every route pulls in, so a per-route CSS cap would be 18 copies of the same number.

TOOLS CHROME RE-DERIVATION (Issue #785, 2026-11-02): the owner restored `PublicNav` and `Breadcrumbs` on both Tools surfaces and abolished the Issue #288 chrome removal (「`/tools` は index・詳細とも PublicNav とパンくずを戻す。 #288 を全面廃止する。」), so the chrome chunks are now part of those two first-paint closures. One `pnpm run build` of the ticket branch measured `/tools/` 649,431 B and `/tools/$slug` 644,912 B; the formula outputs are 655,000 B and 650,000 B, and those are the only two caps this change moved. The added closure is named, not inferred: `assets/PublicNav-*.js` (4,298 B) plus the `Breadcrumbs.styles` chunk and its static imports (`Breadcrumbs.styles.ts`, `Breadcrumbs.tsx`, `route-labels.ts`, 2,999 B), and no other module entered either closure. The rest of each route's delta is the ticket's own code — the redesigned index (two sections, card grid, preview map) and the chrome-subtracting shell — not a leak; `bundle:server-only:check` reports nothing for either route. The same build measured the shared entry chunk at 629,440 B, +2,957 B over the branch point (`0e4d4740`), because TanStack Start's route tree imports the route modules eagerly and both Tools routes were edited; that shell growth pushed four untouched routes over their caps by 0.2–0.4 KiB, so those four caps are re-derived from the same measurement too — `/` 660,279 B -> 665,000 B, `/admin/keys` 640,384 B -> 645,000 B, `/design-system` 680,246 B -> 685,000 B, `/keyboard` 665,200 B -> 670,000 B. Their `+route` figures are unchanged from the branch point (30.1 / 10.7 / 49.6 / 34.9 KiB), which is what says the growth is the shell and not their own code. The same re-derivation covers every other route whose measured value the +2,957 B shell growth pushed across a 5,000 B cap boundary — `/admin` 629,543 B -> 635,000 B, `/admin/` 632,936 B -> 640,000 B, `/admin/images` 639,646 B -> 645,000 B, `/admin/invitations` 638,641 B -> 645,000 B, `/admin/login` 634,919 B -> 640,000 B, `/portfolio/` 669,075 B -> 675,000 B — so every cap in this file is once again the formula output of one measurement. `/projects/dotfiles` is NOT re-derived here: the base branch now carries Issue #802's re-derivation of that one route (640,000 B, from `ceil(635184 * 1.0035 / 5000) * 5000`), and this branch keeps that value unchanged. That matters because two `validate` jobs on the SAME commit measured different entry chunks (`index-2J0KjYJT.js`, shell 614.7 KiB, and `index-Cq6DKF8c.js`, shell 615.0 KiB): the build is not byte-identical across runners, and a cap that sits within a few hundred bytes of its measurement is a coin flip. A formula cap keeps 0.35% headroom (~2.2 KB at this size), which is what absorbs that variance.

SHARED CSS RE-DERIVATION (Issue #785, 2026-11-02): the CSS cap is one number because the initial stylesheet is one asset every route pulls in, and the gate measures the pull-request MERGE commit (base + branch), not the branch alone. That merge measured initial_css_bytes = 50,308 B against 50,000 (CI run 41322419730, source sha `1acc5f74`; reproduced locally by extracting `git merge-tree origin/release-0-8-1 HEAD` and running the same build), and rule-level work that changes nothing on screen brought it to 50,204 B. The branch's net addition is therefore 298 B: 7 rules added (411 B) and 4 rules removed (113 B), measured by diffing the built stylesheet of `origin/release-0-8-1` (49,909 B) against the built merge. Added, each with the call site that makes it used: `flex:1 1 auto` 30 B (tools.$slug.tsx frame area and iframe — the base stylesheet has exactly one flex utility, `.flex_1{flex:1 1 0%}`, whose basis is 0% rather than auto); `grid-auto-rows:1fr` 33 B (the index card grid and planned grid — the base has no `grid-auto-rows` rule; it is the measured fix for the 22.4 px card-height difference); `min-height:100dvh` 33 B and `min-height:0` 36 B (the chrome-subtracting column and frame area — the base's min-heights are 100%, 13px and size tokens, `vh` does not subtract mobile browser chrome, and nothing else provides 0); `text-underline-offset:3px` 37 B (declared on the card title instead of inside `_hover`, which is why it is one plain utility and not a second compound hover selector); and the two card-hover rules — `text-decoration:underline` 118 B and the CTA colour 124 B — the affordance the file's own contract specifies now that a card may not use a border or a shadow. Removed: `margin:0 0 2` (23 B), `margin:0 0 4` (23 B), `margin-block-end:var(--spacing-12)` (44 B) and `opacity:.85` (23 B), which the previous index markup used and the redesign does not. Nothing here is dead CSS: Panda emits a utility only when a scanned source references it, and every added rule has the call site listed above. The 204 B still above the old cap was NOT shaved because it would mean deleting the hover affordance (242 B of the 298 B) to buy 0.08% of headroom, still below this policy's 0.35%. The stronger fact is that the old cap was already stale for the BASE branch: 49,909 B x 1.0035 = 50,084 B > 50,000 B, so `release-0-8-1` on its own no longer satisfied the headroom rule and any branch stacked on it would have failed this gate. The formula output is the same for the base tree and for the merge — `ceil(49909 * 1.0035 / 5000) * 5000` = `ceil(50204 * 1.0035 / 5000) * 5000` = 55,000 B — and that is the new shared CSS cap. It relaxes the CSS ceiling for all 18 routes by 5,000 B; the JS caps in this file are unaffected by this change.

WHY THE CAPS MOVED DOWN (Issue #724): the previous caps were derived from a shell that carried ~1.06 MB of server-only code. The Better Auth **server** stack (the core package, Kysely, Drizzle, the SQLite dialects, the API-key plugin) was reachable from the client bundle through four admin modules' module-level imports, and `emoji-picker-react` (335 KB) was pulled into the shared entry chunk because its `EmojiStyle` / `Theme` string enums were imported as values, which defeated the `lazy()` split that was supposed to keep the picker out of first paint. The entry chunk is now 626,488 B — down 1,063,742 B (−63%) — and the picker is a separate lazy chunk. Every cap in this file is the formula output of that measurement, so every cap moved down; the CSS cap did not move (its formula output is unchanged).

WHAT KEEPS THE SHELL SMALL NOW: a byte budget can say HOW BIG a chunk is, not WHAT is in it, so it can only react to a leak by a size delta — and the historical response to a leak was to raise the cap, seven times. `scripts/check-client-bundle-server-only.mjs` (Issue #724, `pnpm run bundle:server-only:check`, declared in `quality/client-bundle-policy.json`) closes that loop: it reads the same build graph, names the module that leaked, and fails. A leak is now a named failure to fix, not a number to renegotiate.

MEASURED BYTES come from the files Rollup emitted (`writeBundle` in `vite.config.ts` -> `scripts/_client-bundle-graph.mjs`), so a cap is compared against the exact bytes a browser downloads — including the preload marker and dependency map that Vite injects after an ordinary user plugin's `generateBundle` runs. Because the entry shell is shared, a base merge that adds a few hundred bytes to the shell re-derives several route caps at once; that is why a release merge turns this gate red until the caps are re-measured with `pnpm run build && pnpm run bundle:budget:check`. It is the gate doing its job, not a flaky test. Raising a cap is not machine-checked (only an `exception` is), so a cap change is expected to carry its measurement and rationale in the PR diff.

tool_iframe.reason: Each Tool is an independent Vite build loaded inside a sandboxed iframe from /tools/<slug>/app/, so its bytes are never part of a host route's first paint. Capping it separately keeps one heavy Tool from being hidden by the host route budget and stops a Tool from inflating the host measurement. The cap is the observed `prototype` bundle (1,502,757 B JS / 8,415 B CSS) plus headroom; the Tool's own repository owns any reduction.
